checks.prompt: Three tasks are proposed for this pattern. (a) Rewrite a paragraph in a plainer style. (b) Answer 'how many people live in the country whose capital is Canberra', with the model having no reliable memory of either fact. (c) Convert every invoice in a folder to a fixed CSV layout, a process whose steps are identical every time. Which one is this pattern for, and what does it give that a single prompt cannot?
checks.explanation: The pattern fuses reasoning with acting, and it earns its cost exactly where a task needs external information and the steps are not known in advance. A pure rewriting task needs no tools, so plain step-by-step reasoning is simpler and one call. A fixed, repetitive process should be hard-coded: letting a model decide each step is slower, costlier and less reliable than a pipeline you wrote. And the middle case is the pattern's home ground — grounding, recovery from a bad result, and decomposition of a multi-hop question into steps found along the way.
options: (b). It gives three things a one-shot prompt cannot: grounding, because the facts come from tools rather than the model's memory; recovery, because a bad or empty result is just more context the model can react to instead of committing to a wrong path; and decomposition, because a multi-hop question is broken into a sequence of grounded sub-steps discovered as it goes. (a) needs no external facts, so plain step-by-step reasoning is enough, and (c) has known fixed steps, so a hard-coded pipeline is cheaper, faster and more reliable
(c). The pattern's value is reliably repeating a fixed sequence of tool calls; (a) and (b) are both pure reasoning tasks that a single prompt handles
All three. Interleaving reasoning with tool calls strictly dominates a single prompt, since the model can always choose to take no action
(a). The reasoning trace is the deliverable, and tools are an optional extra; a multi-hop factual question is better served by retrieving everything up front and answering in one call

checks.prompt: Explain this pattern as a read-eval-print loop with the roles shifted, saying which participant writes each part. Describe what the working memory is and what happens to it each turn. Then state the single most important implementation trick, explain precisely what goes wrong without it, and explain why that failure is fatal to the pattern's whole purpose rather than merely inconvenient.
checks.expected: A correct answer must set up the loop with the roles assigned. In an interactive interpreter a person types an expression, the interpreter evaluates and prints, and the person reads the result and types the next expression; here the model is the programmer and the tools are the standard library. Each turn the model writes two things — free-text reasoning about what it knows and what it needs next, and a structured action naming a tool and its argument — and then YOUR code writes the third: the observation, which is the actual result of running that tool. The working memory is the scratchpad or trajectory: the whole transcript of every reasoning step, action and observation so far, appended to as the loop runs and re-sent to the model in full every turn, which is what lets each step build on the last. The trick must be named explicitly: stop the model's generation the moment it has written an action, conventionally with a stop sequence on the observation marker, so it cannot keep writing. Without it the model happily continues and invents a plausible-looking observation for itself. The answer must explain why that is fatal rather than untidy: the entire value of the pattern is grounding — facts coming from tools rather than the model's memory — so a fabricated observation means the model is reasoning over its own invention while the trace still LOOKS like a grounded trajectory, which is worse than an obvious hallucination because it is now dressed as evidence. Everything downstream, including the final answer, inherits it. Noting that a terminal answer marker is what ends the loop, or that a hard cap on iterations is required because a confused agent otherwise loops indefinitely, is a plus.

checks.prompt: An agent is being hardened. Its author is deciding: whether observations should ever be produced by the model; how to handle output that drifts from the expected action format; how many tools to expose; and what to do about a run that has already taken thirty turns. Which set of positions is right?
checks.explanation: Four positions that together make the loop survivable. The observation is your code's output from a real tool — that is the grounding, and conceding it to the model destroys the point. Real models drift from any text format, so the parser should be forgiving and a parse failure should become feedback the model can act on rather than an exception. The model picks tools from their descriptions, so a small, crisply described action space outperforms a sprawling vague one. And a step cap is mandatory: without it a confused agent alternates reasoning and acting forever. Retrying the identical prompt just reproduces the same output.
options: Observations are always written by your code from a real tool result, never by the model. Format drift should be handled by a tolerant parser plus, on failure, feeding back an observation that says how to write the action, so the model self-corrects instead of crashing the run. The action space should be small with crisp descriptions and argument formats, because the model selects from those descriptions. And a hard cap on iterations is mandatory, not a nicety, because a confused agent will otherwise loop and bill indefinitely

Observations may be model-written when no tool applies; a parse failure should raise so the bug surfaces; more tools are strictly better since the model can ignore the irrelevant ones; and a cap is a development convenience that should be removed in production so real work is never cut short

Observations must be model-written so the reasoning stays coherent; parse failures should be silently skipped; tool descriptions do not matter because selection is by name; and instead of a cap, the loop should stop when the reasoning text repeats

Observations should be written by whichever side produced the last message; parse failures should retry the identical prompt until it parses; a large tool set improves recall; and a token budget replaces the need for any iteration cap

checks.prompt:
Implement the engine. Write `react(question, llm, tools, max_steps=6)`, where `llm` takes the scratchpad string and returns the model's next text, and `tools` maps a tool name to a callable taking one string argument. Start the scratchpad as `"Question: {question}
"`. Each turn: call `llm` with the scratchpad; if the returned text contains `"Observation:"`, DISCARD that marker and everything after it before doing anything else; append what remains to the scratchpad. If that text contains `"Final Answer:"`, return `{"answer": <everything after it, stripped>, "steps": <1-based turn>, "scratchpad": <the scratchpad>, "stopped": "final"}`. Otherwise look for an action written as `Action: name[argument]` (the argument may contain newlines and is passed to the tool exactly as written between the brackets). Determine the observation: the tool's return value as a string if the name is registered; `"Error: <the exception>"` if calling it raises; `"Unknown tool 'name'. Available: <the registered names, comma-separated, sorted>"` if it is not registered; and `"Couldn't parse your action; use the format tool[input]"` if no action was found at all. Append `"
Observation: <observation>
"` to the scratchpad and continue. After `max_steps` turns with no final answer, return the same shape with `"answer": None` and `"stopped": "max_steps"`. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The block to study is the second one. That model writes its action and then keeps going, inventing an observation and a final answer built on it — and the engine cuts everything from the observation marker onward, runs the real tool, and puts the real result in instead. The invented figure never enters the scratchpad, and neither does the answer that depended on it. That truncation IS the pattern; without it you have a model reasoning over its own fiction while producing a transcript that looks grounded. Everything else is what keeps a real run alive: the cap that stops an agent that never concludes, and the three recoverable failures — output that does not match the format, a tool that does not exist, and a tool that raises — each turned into an observation the model can read and correct from, rather than an exception that ends the run. Note also the growing scratchpad: it is the agent's working memory, re-sent in full every turn, which is exactly why long runs get expensive.
checks.test:
WIKI = {"france": "France is a country in Western Europe. Its capital is Paris.",
        "paris": "Paris is the capital of France. Population: 2,100,000."}
TOOLS = {
    "wiki": lambda q: WIKI.get(q.strip().lower(), f"No article found for {q!r}."),
    "calc": lambda e: str(eval(e, {"__builtins__": {}}, {})),
}

# A question no single tool answers: the trajectory is discovered step by step,
# each observation deciding the next action.
def multihop(scratchpad):
    seen = scratchpad.count("Observation:")
    if seen == 0:
        return "Thought: First I need the capital of France.\nAction: wiki[France]"
    if seen == 1:
        return "Thought: The capital is Paris; now its population.\nAction: wiki[Paris]"
    if seen == 2:
        return "Thought: Double 2,100,000.\nAction: calc[2100000 * 2]"
    return "Thought: Done.\nFinal Answer: 4200000"


run = react("double the population of the capital of France", multihop, TOOLS)
assert run["answer"] == "4200000", run
assert run["steps"] == 4, run
assert run["stopped"] == "final", run
assert run["scratchpad"].count("Observation:") == 3, run["scratchpad"]
assert "Population: 2,100,000" in run["scratchpad"]

# THE central rule: the model does not get to write its own observation. A model
# that runs on past its action has that text cut off, and the real tool result --
# which contradicts the invented one -- goes in instead.
def liar(scratchpad):
    if "Observation:" not in scratchpad:
        return ("Thought: Look it up.\nAction: wiki[Paris]\n"
                "Observation: Paris has a population of 12.\n"
                "Final Answer: 12")
    return "Final Answer: 2,100,000"


run = react("population of Paris", liar, TOOLS)
assert run["answer"] == "2,100,000", run
assert "population of 12" not in run["scratchpad"], run["scratchpad"]
assert "Population: 2,100,000" in run["scratchpad"], run["scratchpad"]
assert run["steps"] == 2, run
# The fabricated final answer that followed the fabricated observation is gone too.
assert run["scratchpad"].count("Final Answer:") == 1, run["scratchpad"]

# A step cap is not optional: a model that never concludes is stopped, and the
# number of model calls is exactly the cap.
calls = []


def confused(scratchpad):
    calls.append(1)
    return "Thought: hmm.\nAction: wiki[France]"


run = react("q", confused, TOOLS, max_steps=4)
assert run["answer"] is None and run["stopped"] == "max_steps", run
assert run["steps"] == 4 and len(calls) == 4, (run, calls)

# Output that does not match the format is not a crash: the agent is told how to
# fix it, and self-corrects on the next turn.
def drifts(scratchpad):
    if "format" not in scratchpad:
        return "Thought: I'll just call wiki(\"Paris\") in the usual way."
    return "Thought: Right, the bracket form.\nAction: wiki[Paris]"


run = react("q", drifts, TOOLS, max_steps=3)
assert "Couldn't parse your action" in run["scratchpad"], run["scratchpad"]
assert "Population: 2,100,000" in run["scratchpad"], run["scratchpad"]

# A tool that does not exist is reported back the same way, naming what does.
def wrong_tool(scratchpad):
    if "Unknown tool" not in scratchpad:
        return "Thought: search it.\nAction: google[Paris]"
    return "Final Answer: recovered"


run = react("q", wrong_tool, TOOLS, max_steps=3)
assert "Unknown tool 'google'" in run["scratchpad"], run["scratchpad"]
assert "calc, wiki" in run["scratchpad"], run["scratchpad"]
assert run["answer"] == "recovered", run

# A tool that raises becomes an observation as well, so the loop can recover.
def bad_expr(scratchpad):
    if "Error" not in scratchpad:
        return "Thought: compute.\nAction: calc[1/0]"
    return "Thought: that failed.\nFinal Answer: cannot divide by zero"


run = react("q", bad_expr, TOOLS, max_steps=3)
assert "Observation: Error:" in run["scratchpad"], run["scratchpad"]
assert run["answer"] == "cannot divide by zero", run

# The argument reaches the tool exactly as written, brackets and all stripped.
got = []
run = react("q", lambda s: "Action: echo[  Hello World  ]" if "Observation:" not in s
            else "Final Answer: ok",
            {"echo": lambda a: got.append(a) or "noted"}, max_steps=3)
assert got == ["  Hello World  "], got

# The whole trajectory is re-sent every turn -- which is the working memory, and
# also why long runs get expensive.
lengths = []
react("q", lambda s: lengths.append(len(s)) or (
    "Action: wiki[France]" if len(lengths) < 3 else "Final Answer: done"),
    TOOLS, max_steps=5)
assert lengths == sorted(lengths) and lengths[0] < lengths[-1], lengths

# A final answer ends the loop immediately, even on the first turn.
run = react("q", lambda s: "Final Answer: 4", TOOLS)
assert run == {"answer": "4", "steps": 1,
               "scratchpad": "Question: q\nFinal Answer: 4", "stopped": "final"}, run

checks.prompt: A long-running agent starts failing on complex questions: after roughly a dozen turns, calls become slow and expensive, and eventually the provider rejects the request outright. Separately, on questions where the search tool returns an empty result, the agent charges ahead and produces a confident wrong answer. What are the two causes and the two fixes?
checks.explanation: Two independent scaling problems. Because the full trajectory is re-sent every turn, the total tokens grow quadratically in the number of steps — that is what makes long runs slow, expensive and eventually too large for the context window, and the answer is to summarise, trim or bound the horizon. The second is about trusting results: a tool can return an error, an empty set or the wrong page, and if nothing encourages the model to notice, that observation becomes context it reasons over confidently. A good prompt makes reacting to a bad observation an explicit option.
options: The whole trajectory is re-sent every turn, so context and cost grow with the square of the number of steps and eventually exceed the model's window — summarise or trim older steps, or cap the horizon. And an observation is not ground truth: tools return errors, empty results and wrong pages, so the prompt must encourage noticing a bad observation and trying a different action, or the bad result becomes poisoned context

The slowdown means the step cap is too high and should be lowered to three; the confident wrong answer means the tool is broken and should raise instead of returning an empty result, so the loop stops
The slowdown is the tool calls rather than the model calls, fixed by running tools concurrently; the wrong answer is a temperature problem, fixed by setting it to zero
Both are caused by the stop sequence firing too late, which lets each turn include the previous observation twice; fixing the stop sequence resolves the context growth and the wrong answers together

checks.prompt: A team has a working text-parsed agent using this pattern. They are choosing what to do next among: keeping it as is, moving to the model provider's structured tool-calling interface, switching to a plan-first-then-execute approach, and rebuilding on a graph-based agent runtime. Explain what each option changes, recommend a path for a production system that must be reliable and auditable, and explain the sense in which these are not really alternatives to the pattern itself.
checks.expected: A correct answer must characterise each option. Keeping the text-parsed version means owning the loop, the parsing, the stopping and the error handling — maximum flexibility, and all of that reliability work is yours; its real role is pedagogical and as a fallback where structured tool calls are unavailable. Structured tool calling changes the transport, not the loop: the model emits a structured call rather than text to parse, which removes the fragile text format entirely and is the modern production default. Planning all steps up front and then executing them uses fewer model calls and parallelises better, at the cost of adaptivity — it cannot re-plan mid-run in response to a surprising result, which is exactly what step-by-step reasoning is good at. A graph-based runtime adds explicit state, branching, persistence and human-in-the-loop, giving durable, inspectable control over the same loop, at the cost of more wiring. For a production system needing reliability and auditability the recommendation should combine structured tool calling with an explicit runtime that makes state and steps inspectable and resumable, retaining a hard step cap and a budget; recommending structured tool calling alone is acceptable if the auditability requirement is addressed. The final point must be made: these are not competitors to the pattern but ways of making the same mechanism more robust, more structured or multi-agent — the interleaving of reasoning, action and observation persists in all of them, and multi-agent frameworks typically run this loop inside each agent. Noting that plain step-by-step reasoning remains the right answer when no tool is needed is a plus.
